newsitem.title: USA: No U.S. cash management bill seen in Jan - analysts.
newsitem.headline: No U.S. cash management bill seen in Jan - analysts.

text.p: It may not be until mid-February that another cash management bill is offered by the Treasury, analysts said, thanks to less-than-anticipated government outlays.

"The next interval we're looking at is a large interest rate payment in mid-February. There are no major tax payments in February, so that's when the government is likely to need the money," said William Sullivan, director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
The Treasury came out of December with a total cash balance of $32.8 billion, more than the government had projected in a late October press conference.
Sullivan said spending in the "other withdrawals, unclassified" category were down about $5.0 billion from original government projections and that Medicare expenses were $1.2 billion lower.

Also lending support to the notion the Treasury would refrain from CMB issuance in coming weeks was the fact that the size of the weekly bills auction has been cut $3.0 billion from the $28.0 billion level it was at about a month ago.
"The cash balances look pretty good. They probably won't have to do anything until the February refunding," agreed Kim Rupert, economist at MMS International.
She also noted that government outlays weren't as large as anticipated, but cautioned legislative changes could affect the budgetary process.

Elliott Platt, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said he expected the Congressional Budget Office to annouce that the baseline budget deficit in upcoming fiscal years would be smaller than previously estimated. As a consequence, he said, fewer outlay reductions would be needed.
And Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc, said he does not expect any CMBs in January.
"We see the U.S. economy performing well in the first half of the year, so a trend of healthy government revenues should continue," he said.
Iggo said the U.S. economy likely would grow between 1.0 percent and 3.0 percent in 1997.
